MAINE SUPREME JUDICIAL COURT Reporter of Decisions Decision: 2026 ME 97 Docket: And-25-463 Argued: June 2, 2026 Decided: September 15, 2026
Panel: STANFILL, C.J., and MEAD, CONNORS, LAWRENCE, DOUGLAS, LIPEZ, and TAUB, JJ.
STATE OF MAINE
v.
JAMES R. FOOTMAN JR.
TAUB, J. [¶1] James R. Footman Jr. appeals from a judgment of conviction of robbery (Class A), 17-A M.R.S § 651 (1)(E) (2026), and of violation of condition of release (Class E), 15 M.R.S. § 1092(1)(A) (2026), entered by the trial court (Androscoggin County, Archer, J.) after a jury trial. Footman also appeals from his sentence. [¶2] The convictions pertain to a robbery on November 11, 2024. Footman contends that the court clearly erred or abused its discretion by admitting evidence relating to a similar robbery on November 14 , for which Footman was not on trial. Because evidence of the November 14 robbery was not probative of the identity of the person who committed the robbery on November 11, the court erred in admitting it. Because we determine that the 2 error was not harmless, we vacate the judgment of conviction and do not reach the sentence appeal. I. BACKGROUND A. Factual Background [¶3] “Viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the State, the jury rationally could have found the following facts beyond a reasonable doubt.” State v. Ellis, 2025 ME 56, ¶ 3, 339 A.3d 794. [¶4] On November 11, 2024, an individual wearing a medical mask and black Nike shoes with white trim walked into a Big Apple store on Main Street in Lewiston. entry.title: US Supreme Court Upholds Right to Vote by Mail
entry.content:
AUGUSTA, MAINE – Absentee voting by mail will continue just as it has in prior elections, announced Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today.  The US Supreme Court rejected the US Postal Service and Trump Administration’s quest to change the rules for mailed ballots.  States including the State of Maine had filed a lawsuit to challenge the Trump Executive Order and US Postal Service rule that would have dramatically limited the ability of clerks to mail ballots to voters.  A lower court blocked the rule on constitutional grounds, and the US Supreme Court denied the Trump Administration’s attempt to overturn the lower court.

“This is good news for voters and for democracy.  Voters can rest assured that they have all of the same options for absentee voting including receiving and returning their ballot by mail that they have had in every other election,” said Secretary of State Shenna Bellows.  “We know that many Mainers – particularly seniors and people with disabilities – appreciate the convenience of voting from home, and we are thrilled that our joint legal efforts with states across the country to protect the right to vote by mail have succeeded.”

Voters can request absentee ballots utilizing the Secretary of State’s online absentee ballot portal, in writing, or by calling their municipal clerk directly. Absentee voting in Maine begins October 5, and voters should start receiving their ballots in the mail in the first week of October. Voters can track the status of their absentee ballot via Maine’s online absentee ballot tracking portal.

Panel: STANFILL, C.J., and MEAD, CONNORS, LAWRENCE, DOUGLAS, and LIPEZ, JJ. Majority: STANFILL, C.J., and MEAD, CONNORS, LAWRENCE, DOUGLAS, and LIPEZ, JJ. Concurrence: STANFILL, C.J.
STATE OF MAINE
v.
WILLIAM BRADBURY
LAWRENCE, J. [¶1] William Bradbury appeals from a judgment of conviction of one count of unlawful sexual touching (Class D), 17-A M.R.S. § 260(1)(A) (2023),1 and two counts of indecent conduct (Class E), 17-A M.R.S. § 854 (2026), entered by the trial court (Piscataquis County, Haddow, J.) after a jury trial. This amendment changed the language of the statute from “has not expressly or impliedly acquiesced in,” which is at issue in this appeal, to “has not consented to.” To this end, the Legislature defined “consent” to mean “a word or action by a person that indicates a freely given agreement.” P.L. 2023, ch. 280, § 1 (effective Oct. 25, 2023) (codified at 17-A M.R.S. § 251(E-1) (2026)). 2 conviction; and (2) the trial court abused its discretion by allowing the State to use evidence that it had not timely provided to Bradbury in discovery for the purposes of cross-examining Bradbury at trial. entry.title: Protecting Maine Through Stronger Infrastructure and Climate Resiliency
entry.content:
Hello, this is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

You know, when I took office nearly eight years ago, I promised that Maine won't wait to take action to protect our state, our people, and our economy from the dangers of extreme weather events caused by pollution and changes to our environment. And I promised that we would fight to preserve this special place that we call home; preserve it for the benefit of our children and grandchildren.

The stakes could not be higher. Look no further than the devastating storms of just a few years ago. Storms that impacted our communities, our people, and our economy—that destroyed a lot of infrastructure across the state.

I've made climate action a cornerstone of my Administration. First, we created the Maine Climate Council, and we issued a groundbreaking climate action plan. And we dedicated millions of federal and state dollars to make that plan a reality.

In 2025, we made the single largest investment in storm recovery by any administration in Maine history, and we created the State Resilience Office to build better, stronger public infrastructure to withstand future storms.

That office manages a partnership of more than 300 communities and has awarded more than $29 million in state and federal funds for projects to prepare local communities for flooding, for storm surge, for rising sea levels, and other climate and weather events that put people's lives and livelihoods at risk.

Recently, I was proud to announce the latest round of funding through that partnership: more than $4.7 million in grants to 72 cities and Tribal Governments, including the towns of Bingham and Madawaska:

  • The Town of Bingham will install high-efficiency heat pumps and a rooftop solar system in order to lower their energy costs at the municipally owned Veterans Building;
  • The Town of Madawaska will use their grant to launch the RIDER Program, a shared e-bike fleet in a rural community that doesn't have public transportation;
  • And the Town of Freedom will use its grant to do an energy audit of its buildings and to plan for a bridge replacement across Hustus Brook.

Through these projects and so many more, we are continuing to address the very real threat of severe weather events for the health of our people, the health of our environment, and the health of our economy.

You know that clean air and clean water know no political party. Our planet is neither Democratic nor Republican. It's the home of all of us, and it is the responsibility of all of us and all governments to preserve it for future generations.

I am proud that over the past nearly eight years, we've made cost-effective heat pumps, weatherization programs, and other things available for Maine people and businesses. We've attracted investments in emerging industries and renewables, and we've created good-paying, green collar jobs. We've reduced our reliance on expensive fossil fuels, and we've mobilized scientists, industry leaders, local and state officials, and young people from all over to act as one to address the effects of climate change.

We won't wait for the next storm or the next disaster. We do care. And as the author Wendell Berry wrote, "We care for this home that is ours. A home that we care for as we care for no other place in the world."

This is Governor Janet Mills, and thank you for listening.

entry.content:
Friday, September 18, 2026

UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT

DISTRICT OF MAINE

**PRESS RELEASE**

NATURALIZATION CEREMONY CELEBRATED

September 18, 2026

 

On September 18, 2026, U.S. District Judge Stacey D. Neumann commemorated Citizenship and Constitution Day with a special ceremony at the University of Southern Maine in Portland.

The Honorable Stacey D. Neumann presided and administered the oath of citizenship to forty-one new citizens from twenty-five different countries, including Angola, Bangladesh, Brazil, Burundi, Cambodia, Canada, Central African Republic, China, Columbia, Democratic Republic of Congo, Costa Rica, Djibouti, France, Greece, Hungary, India, Iraq, Kazakhstan, South Korea, Lithuania, Rwanda, South Sudan, Spain, the United Kingdom, and Vietnam.

A copy of Judge Neumann’s remarks are posted on the Court’s website.
